chapters.title: Chapter 2: Intangible Assets: Brands, Patents, and Licences

lessons.title: Brand Power and Pricing Power: Lessons from Indian Consumer Leaders

body.text: A brand is not a moat because people recognise it. It is a moat only when customers keep buying it after you raise the price.

children.text: India has hundreds of famous consumer brands. Very few of them are genuine economic moats. The difference comes down to one measurable ability: pricing power. Warren Buffett has described pricing power as the single most important factor in evaluating a business, adding that if a company has to hold a prayer session before raising prices even slightly, it is a terrible business. This lesson shows you how to test for it.
Why Customers Pay More for a Brand
A brand creates economic value only when it solves a real problem for the customer. In India, three problems matter most.

body.caption: Three ways a brand creates pricing power

cells: The product is a small part of a big decision, or a mistake is expensive and visible, so customers will not risk an unknown name
Tanishq (Titan) in gold jewellery, where purity is hard for a buyer to verify; Asian Paints, where repainting a home costs far more than the paint
Low-ticket, frequently bought items where comparing alternatives is not worth the customer's time
Maggi (Nestle India), Colgate toothpaste, Britannia biscuits
The person choosing the product is not the one paying, and they trust a familiar name
Fevicol (Pidilite), which carpenters have long recommended and used; paint brands pushed by contractors and dealers

body.text: Notice what is missing: "the product is better". A better product can be copied. Trust, habit, and influencer loyalty take years or decades to build, and that time is what a competitor with money cannot buy.

children.text: Pricing Power: The Only Test That Counts

markDefs.definition: The percentage change in quantity demanded for a 1% change in price. Low elasticity means customers barely react to price increases, which is what a strong brand creates.

children.text: The cleanest test of brand strength arrives when input costs spike: palm oil for soaps and snacks, crude derivatives for paints, gold for jewellery. A company with real pricing power passes the higher cost to customers with little loss of volume. A company without it must choose between shrinking margins and losing customers. Economists call the customer's sensitivity to price
price elasticity of demand
Worked Example: A 10% Input Cost Shock

Three hypothetical companies each have sales of ₹100 crore and raw material costs of ₹50 crore, a 50% gross margin. Input costs then rise 10%, pushing raw material cost to ₹55 crore at the same volume.

body.caption: Same cost shock, three different outcomes (₹ crore)
headers: Weak brand: holds price, volume flat

cells: Change in gross profit vs ₹50 crore

children.text: The strong brand ends the year with more gross profit than before the shock. Both weak brands lose, whether they raise prices and lose customers or protect volume and absorb the cost. That asymmetry, repeated every inflation cycle for decades, is what pricing power is worth.
Strong brand: Sales = ₹100 crore × 1.08 × 0.99 = ₹106.92 crore. Raw material = ₹55 crore × 0.99 = ₹54.45 crore. Gross profit = ₹52.47 crore, up 4.9% from ₹50 crore.
Weak brand raising price: Sales = ₹100 crore × 1.08 × 0.88 = ₹95.04 crore. Raw material = ₹55 crore × 0.88 = ₹48.40 crore. Gross profit = ₹46.64 crore, down 6.7%.
Weak brand holding price: Sales = ₹100 crore. Raw material = ₹55 crore. Gross profit = ₹45 crore, down 10%.
Raw material cost scales with volume, while sales scale with both price and volume. That is why a small volume loss matters so much less than a large one.

body.title: Calculate the Pricing Power Payoff
body.prompt: A consumer company has sales of ₹1,000 crore and raw material costs of ₹600 crore. Input costs rise 10%, so raw material cost at the same volume becomes ₹660 crore. The company raises prices by 7% and loses 2% of volume. What is its new gross profit, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: Sales = ₹1,000 crore × 1.07 × 0.98 = ₹1,048.6 crore. Raw material = ₹660 crore × 0.98 = ₹646.8 crore. Gross profit = ₹1,048.6 crore − ₹646.8 crore = ₹401.8 crore, slightly above the original ₹400 crore. The price increase fully protected gross profit.

children.text: Brand Resilience: The Maggi Test
The ultimate test of a brand is whether customers come back after something goes badly wrong. Nestle India faced exactly that in 2015.

events.title: FSSAI orders Maggi withdrawn
events.description: India's food regulator bans Maggi noodles over alleged lead and MSG labelling issues. Nestle India recalls and destroys product worth hundreds of crores, and India's best-known instant noodle vanishes from shelves.

events.title: Bombay High Court sets aside the ban
events.description: The court overturns the ban and orders fresh testing of samples.

events.title: Maggi relaunches
events.description: After samples clear testing, Maggi returns to stores.

events.title: Leadership regained
events.description: Despite rivals using the gap to push their own noodles, Maggi recovers its position as the market leader in instant noodles.

children.text: Competitors had five months of empty shelves to steal Maggi's customers, and still could not keep them. Decades of habit and trust, especially among families who grew up with the product, proved more durable than a regulatory crisis. A brand that survives that kind of shock is doing real economic work.
How to Spot Pricing Power in the Numbers
Stable gross margins through inflation:

on Screener.in, expand the expenses line in the Profit & Loss section to see material cost as a percentage of sales. Check it through high-inflation years such as FY22 and FY23. A brand with pricing power recovers its margin within a few quarters.
Price-led growth that does not kill volume:
management commentary and results presentations of listed FMCG companies usually split growth into volume and price. Price increases alongside steady or positive volume growth are the signal.
Consistently high ROCE:
brand-driven consumer companies with real moats tend to show ROCE far above the 15% pre-tax hurdle for many years, often because they need relatively little capital to grow.
Advertising that sustains rather than props up:

check advertising and promotion spend as a percentage of sales in the annual report. A strong brand keeps it steady. A brand that needs ever-higher ad spend and discounts to hold share is fighting, not dominating.

body.label: The one-question brand test
body.value: If this company raised prices 10% tomorrow, would most customers keep buying?
body.context: If the honest answer is yes, the brand may be a moat. If they would switch to a rival or a private label, it is only a famous name.

body.title: Which Brand Has More Pricing Power?
body.question: Which of these situations best indicates strong brand-based pricing power?
options: A beverage brand grew revenue 25% after doubling its advertising budget and running heavy discounts
A paint company raised prices several times during a raw material spike, and its volume growth stayed positive
A new snack brand became the most followed food brand on Instagram in India
An electronics brand has the highest unit market share in its category because it is the cheapest
body.explanation: Only option B shows customers accepting higher prices without walking away. Option A buys growth with spending and discounts. Option C is awareness, not pricing power. Option D wins on price, which is the opposite of a brand premium.

body.title: Two Jewellery Retailers
body.scenario: You are comparing two listed jewellery retailers. Retailer A is a national brand with a long record on purity and hallmarking and consistent same-store sales growth. Retailer B is a fast-growing regional chain that offers lower making charges than A and heavy festive discounts. Both have similar revenue growth over the last three years. Gold prices have risen sharply during this period.
body.prompt: Which retailer is more likely to have brand-based pricing power, and what data would you check to confirm it?
body.modelAnswer: Retailer A is more likely to have pricing power, because jewellery is a high-value purchase where purity is hard for the buyer to verify, so trust matters more than a small price difference. Retailer B is winning on price, which a competitor can match. To confirm: compare gross margins and making charge levels over several years, especially whether A kept margins steady without matching B's discounts; check same-store sales growth, which separates brand pull from store openings; look at ROCE through the cycle; and read management commentary on discounting during festive seasons. If A holds margins while B has to keep discounting to grow, the brand is doing economic work.

body.title: Test One Consumer Brand You Own
steps: Pick one listed consumer company you own directly or through a mutual fund
On Screener.in, note material cost as a percentage of sales for FY21, FY22, FY23, and FY24
Check whether gross margin dipped during the inflation years and how quickly it recovered
Read one results presentation from FY23 and find how much growth came from price versus volume
Find advertising and promotion spend as a percentage of sales in the annual report and check whether it is rising
Answer the one-question brand test honestly, and write down why

body.text: Companies and brands named are used to illustrate concepts from public information and are not investment recommendations. The worked examples use hypothetical figures.

points: A brand is a moat only when it creates pricing power, meaning customers keep buying after prices rise
In India, brands create pricing power by solving three problems: trust where failure is costly, habit and low search cost, and influencer or professional loyalty
Input cost spikes are the real test: a strong brand can grow gross profit through a shock that shrinks a weak brand's gross profit
Maggi's recovery after its 2015 ban shows how durable decades of habit and trust can be
Look for stable gross margins through inflation, price-led growth with steady volume, high ROCE, and steady rather than rising ad spend
Ask the one-question test: would most customers keep buying after a 10% price rise?
